edition.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Internet Archive record of the McGraw-Hill print: date 2002, ISBN 0071385290. The Lessons follow its 15-chapter layout (No Guts, No Glory through A Final Word), confirmed by the chapter headings in a reader's notes on that ISBN (sive.rs) and a chapter summary (bookey.app), and by chapter 1 on the author's site. A 2nd edition appeared in 2023 (McGraw-Hill product page); no Lesson relies on it. The scanned text itself is lending-only and was not read.

rows.claim: Bernstein reminds readers that US stocks lost most of their value from 1929 to 1932.
rows.note: Chapter 1 on the author's site: "from the market peak in September 1929 to the bottom in July 1932, the market lost an astonishing 83% of its value."

rows.claim: This Lesson distils chapter 2, Measuring the Beast; your 25-times-expenses target rests on a sane return estimate.
rows.note: Secondary: reader's notes on ISBN 0071385290 head the section "CH 2 : Measuring the Beast"; the Bookey chapter summary lists "Chapter 2 | Measuring the Beast" too. The 25-times target is the roadmap's figure, not a claim about the book.

rows.claim: Using US data since 1926, Bernstein shows stocks earned about 10 percent a year and long bonds about 5 percent. Treasury bills earned little more than inflation.
rows.note: Chapter 1: "returns of U.S. stocks, long-term Treasury bonds, and Treasury bills since 1900 ... stocks (9.89% annualized), bonds (4.85%), bills (3.86%)", inflation 3.6%. The figures hold but the series starts in 1900, not 1926 (1926 is the start of the small/large and value/growth tables), and it sits in chapter 1. Card now says "Chapter 1's US data since 1900".

rows.claim: Writing in 2002, after the late-1990s boom, Bernstein expected future stock returns well below the historic figure.
rows.note: Secondary, notes on chapter 2: the Gordon equation gives "Dividend growth is 5% and yield is 1.55% = 6.55%. Nowhere near the 10% returns of the past." Publication year 2002 per the Internet Archive record.

rows.claim: For your plan, estimate future returns from yield plus growth, not from the last ten years. A modest number keeps your 25-times target honest.
rows.note: Applied Card. Secondary: "Discount Rate (market return) = Dividend Yield + Dividend Growth". The 25-times target is the roadmap's figure.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils chapters 3 and 4: why you cannot beat the market and how to build a portfolio from whole asset classes; your core is 80 percent index ETFs.
rows.note: Secondary: "CH. 3 : The Market is Smarter Than You Are", "CH. 4 : The Perfect Portfolio"; Bookey lists the same titles. The 80 percent core is the roadmap's figure.

rows.claim: Bernstein walks through the great manias: the South Sea Bubble, the British railway mania of the 1840s, the 1920s boom and the 1990s tech bubble.
rows.note: Secondary (chapter summary of "Chapter 5 | Tops: A History of Manias"): sections on the diving company bubble, the South Sea Bubble, canal mania, railway stocks in the 1840s, the 1920s boom and 1929 crash, the go-go era, the dot-com bubble. The National Post review of 2 November 2002 (https://bylo.org/fp02nov02jc.html) also reports the late-1990s bubble in Part 2. The passage itself was not seen.

rows.claim: In 1979 Business Week ran a cover called The Death of Equities, close to a great time to buy.
rows.note: Author's own text (excerpt of the 2nd edition): "In August 1979, BusinessWeek ran a cover story with the headline 'The Death of Equities'"; stocks then "were cheap, cheap, cheap". Bookey lists a section "The Death of Equities" in chapter 6 of the 15-chapter (1st edition) layout.

rows.claim: Bernstein describes US stocks lagging inflation from the mid-1960s to the early 1980s.
rows.note: Chapter 1: "during the 17 years from 1966 to 1982, stock returns just barely kept up with inflation". Stocks did not lag inflation; the Card now says they barely kept up with it from 1966 to 1982.

rows.claim: Knowing the South Sea Bubble and 2000 helps you hold your index core in the next crash.
rows.note: Applied Card. Secondary: the chapter 5 summary covers the South Sea Bubble and the dot-com bubble; the introduction on the author's site (https://www.efficientfrontier.com/t4poi/intro.htm) says a study of previous manias and crashes gives a fighting chance of recognising them.

rows.claim: In every mania, people claim a new era has made the old valuation rules useless. Bernstein shows that claim was made in the 1920s and the 1990s, and failed both times.
rows.note: Looked for a passage tying a "new era" claim to the 1920s and the 1990s; none found in the sources that could be opened. The Card now says only what the notes on chapter 5 show: "speculative markets in which the old rules seem to go out the window" and John Templeton's warning about "This time, it's different", given as a paraphrase without quotation marks.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils how Bernstein assembles the pillars: estimating what you need and choosing your mix; it turns theory into your actual €40k plan.
rows.note: Secondary: "Chapter 12 | Will You Have Enough?" and "Chapter 13 | Defining Your Mix"; the same titles in the reader's notes. The €40k is the roadmap's figure, not a claim about the book.

rows.claim: He warns that a retiree can safely spend only a few percent of the portfolio each year. That logic sits behind targets such as 25 times annual expenses.
rows.note: Two independent secondary sources. Reader's notes, chapter 12: "Plan on spending, at maximum, the expected real return of your portfolio. (ie: 3%-4% of its value)". Bookey: an income of 40,000 dollars a year at a 4% real return needs a 1 million dollar nest egg (25 times); withdraw around 3% to 4% annually.

rows.claim: In your plan, the 80 percent index core and 20 percent satellite are an allocation decision. Write your stock-and-bond split down before you invest your €40k.
rows.note: Applied Card: the figures are the roadmap's, not the book's. The book side, asset allocation as the main decision, is in the notes on chapter 4: "asset allocation should be the major focus of your investment strategy".
